author: @gittrend.io
title_or_hook: Marimba: typed decisions about live audio from charcot.ai (the run's tool find)
summary: Marimba is an open-source interface that answers typed questions about a short audio window (yes/no, choice, or a calibrated probability score) without producing a transcript: one pass over the last eight seconds of audio serves every question. It is built for voice agents that need to know things like whether someone is speaking or has finished a turn. Primary source checked this run: the arXiv paper 'marimba: A System One Model for Speech' (arXiv:2611.18330, submitted Nov 13, 2026, charcot.ai). The backbone is a FROZEN Qwen3-ASR 0.6B per the paper; the post's on-screen string 'Qwen2-A5R-0.6B' is WRONG against the paper, trust the paper. Lexical questions are scored zero-shot from the ASR decoder's hypotheses with Platt calibration; non-lexical questions use a question-conditioned head, a frozen layer-18 turn-end readout, and layer-12 speaker readouts; language ID reuses the ASR model's own scores. Install reported as pip install marimba-audio; weights Apache-2.0; a Hugging Face Space demo exists per the release coverage. Tasks covered: term spotting, turn end, voice activity, language ID, same speaker, speaker change, speaker count, and personal-information presence, with phonetically confusable hard negatives. The paper reports it matches or beats Qwen3-Omni-30B and Qwen2-Audio-7B on 6 of 9 shared benchmarks. Measured weakness from the paper itself: turn-end AUROC 0.930 versus Smart Turn v3.2 at 0.982 on Smart Turn's own test set, so Marimba is not the best turn-end detector, it is the cheapest general one. Heads do not generalize to unseen task types (one scene task at chance, per coverage). Single-author project, days old (paper Nov 13, HF Daily Papers Nov 17); conversational test sets are partly private (decoder AUROC 0.80-0.92 there, 0.92-0.97 on public read speech). Plugs into agent fleet infrastructure and GSE Content OS: (a) voice-agent turn-taking, returning 'has the speaker finished?' as one calibrated score from a 0.6B frozen backbone instead of a full transcript or a 7B-30B audio-LLM call, the free-first pattern; (b) speaker-change and speaker-count readouts as diarization primitives in front of transcription. Creative angles: the design pattern (one frozen encoding, many typed questions, calibrated outputs) mirrors the GSE reasoning doctrine's one-reasoning-many-signals shape; PII-presence detection as a pre-filter before audio leaves the machine is a Family Shield use the creator never pitched. First test: pip install marimba-audio, run turn-end and speaker-change questions over 20 already-owned audio clips with known endpoints, compare calibration against the current transcript-based path; half an hour, zero cost.
metrics_or_datasets: Turn-end AUROC 0.930 (vs Smart Turn v3.2 at 0.982 on its own test set)
Matches or beats Qwen3-Omni-30B and Qwen2-Audio-7B on 6 of 9 shared benchmarks (paper)
Decoder AUROC 0.80-0.92 on partly private conversational sets; 0.92-0.97 on public read speech
Backbone: frozen Qwen3-ASR 0.6B
engine_training_value: Direct. The typed task suite is a labelled benchmark: term presence, turn end, voice activity, speaker change/count, PII presence, each with hard negatives - training/eval data for any audio-decision head the fleet builds. For the prediction engine itself: none; this trains the fleet's ears, not the model.

author: @therundownai
title_or_hook: Banks: customers liable when third-party AI agents are hacked (Family Shield + fleet headline)
summary: As posted (summarized): Citi, JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America are warning customers they may be held responsible for losses involving third-party AI agents they authorized, including where the tool was hacked or credentials were stolen, with PNC and Citizens issuing similar warnings. Verification this run confirms the substance and adds the mechanism: TechCrunch (Nov 18) reports Citi updated its Online User Agreement (a new Section H) so activity through a third-party agent a customer authorized is treated as the customer's, including credential-leak cases, with no duty to investigate whether the agent followed instructions; JPMorgan and Bank of America moved last month, PNC changed terms the same week, and Citizens emailed customers a similar warning. Independent explainers (Decrypt, AllAboutCookies, Cobo) match. One further bank appears in a detailed contract read (Wells Fargo, a new section effective Mon Nov 24), single-source, noted as such. The carve-out matters: agents the bank itself provides are excluded from the extra liability at Citi; first-party channels keep the old protection, third-party credential-sharing loses it. Federal consumer rules still limit liability for genuinely unauthorized transfers regardless of contract wording (per Decrypt's coverage); the terms shift the starting position, not the whole law. Plugs into Family Shield (exposure/liability lane) and the autonomous revenue engine's operating rules: an agent acting through a bank-approved, limited connection is a different risk class from an agent holding raw login credentials. Pairs with the 2026-11-19 PM JPMorgan vendor-breach dossier: two days, two directions of the same lesson. Creative angles: a one-line Kit/client sales argument with a citation (agent access is now a liability question; sites and automations need an access audit); for the fleet, least-privilege scoped revocable access is now both a security posture and a liability posture. The post compresses five banks' different wordings into one warning; per-bank details come from the coverage, not the post. Nothing here is legal advice; it is a filed news record.
metrics_or_datasets: Citi Online User Agreement new Section H (per TechCrunch, Nov 18)
Wells Fargo new section effective Mon Nov 24 (single-source contract read)
